Every chip that runs AI today has to be perfect. And perfect costs energy.
Lower the voltage and a chip saves power, but its arithmetic starts making random mistakes.
Normal language models can't cope. One hit on a critical number can wreck the whole output.
So MIT researchers trained models on broken hardware, on purpose. Random chunks of the math were dropped every time.
You'd expect bigger models to fall apart faster. Instead, past a certain size, they recover.
That's how good error-correcting codes behave, and how your brain's grid cells track position through noisy neurons.
It's a preprint, tested to about a billion weights. Nobody knows yet if it holds at frontier scale.
If it does, AI could run on cheap, faulty chips using far less energy. Latoon. Voyaging the unseen. Follow for more.
